case_title: Central Bureau of Investigation v. Shyam Bihari & Others
weapon: Fatal injury from a .12 bore gun (not recovered); service rifles (.303) issued to accused; country-made pistol alleged by PW-15
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-3, PW-6, PW-15); circumstantial (GD entries, ballistic report, presence at spot); medical (autopsy); recovery of empty cartridges
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.302/34 IPC; benefit of doubt extended
high_court_outcome: Delay condoned; leave to appeal against acquittal rejected; Government Appeal dismissed (26.07.2012)
neutral_facts: On the night of 24 June 1987, the victim was travelling on a scooter with two companions on a separate scooter toward a village to attend a marriage. Near a road turn at about 9.30 pm, the two companions say that in the scooter light they saw three uniformed men on the road, one carrying a stick and two carrying rifles. The man with the stick flashed a torch at them, and the two scooters skidded. One of the uniformed men allegedly urged others to shoot, and shots were fired. The victim was hit, collapsed, and was taken to a hospital in the presence of police, but died on the way. The two companions escaped to the village. The FIR was lodged by one companion, and a separate case was registered on a rival version describing an armed criminal group and police retaliatory fire, in which two empty cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. Villagers and police arrived at the scene. Three uniformed constables were on patrol that night and had left the police station with rifles and 50 rounds each. Ballistic examination found that some empty cartridges at the spot were fired from the service rifles of two of the constables, while two others were not matched to any of the three. The autopsy showed the fatal injury came from a .12 bore gun, which was not recovered from any of the accused. One witness claimed to have seen the accused fire a country-made pistol, and the accused were said to have remained at the spot after the incident.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a .12 bore gunshot wound
premeditation_planning: Not found; court held no reliable evidence that the exchange of fire was aimed at killing
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent evidence of police action that night; ballistic finding that some cartridges were not from the accused's rifles; autopsy finding of .12 bore gunshot; absence of any identification of the accused
witness_credibility: PW-3 and PW-6 found not helpful against the accused as they could not identify them; PW-15 found unreliable on detailed trial court reasons (late affidavit, identical affidavits, false statement)
post_offence_conduct: Accused allegedly remained at the spot after the incident, which the court held favoured the accused
trial_duration: offence: 24.06.1987; trial judgment: 13.12.2011; High Court: 26.07.2012; Supreme Court: 17.07.2023
legal_representation: Appellant (CBI): Vikramjit Banerjee, ASG, with Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Rajan Kumar Chourasia and others; Respondents: Anil K. Sharma, Sanjeev Kumar, Praveen Chaturvedi
investigation_status: FIR registered; second case (48A/87) registered on rival version; investigation transferred to CB-CID and then CBI; charge-sheet filed; trial completed with 33 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: High Court order described as cryptic; not by itself a ground to remit
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted (13.12.2011). High Court: leave to appeal refused and Government Appeal dismissed (26.07.2012). Supreme Court: CBI appeal dismissed; acquittal stands
prosecution_argument: Deceased shot by uniformed police; presence of accused confirmed by eyewitnesses, ballistic evidence and the cross case; burden on accused to explain; trial court verdict perverse
defence_argument: Witnesses could not identify accused; death from .12 bore weapon not accused's rifle; unmatched cartridges suggest another person; PW-15 unreliable; benefit of doubt correctly given
legal_principle_applied: Appellate court may reappreciate evidence but must not disturb a plausible acquittal not vitiated by ignorance or misreading of evidence; circumstantial case needs a complete chain pointing to the accused alone
